`val` fixes the reference while `var` allows reassignment, and neither says anything about whether the object itself can change.

- **val** — read-only reference (like Java's `final`). The binding cannot be reassigned; the object behind it may still be mutable.
- **var** — mutable reference. Can be reassigned.

Idiomatic Kotlin defaults to val — IDE inspections suggest var → val whenever a variable is never reassigned. Writing `var` should be a deliberate decision, since immutability is a thread-safety and correctness win.

Both are statically typed; inference is the rule and explicit annotations are reserved for public API and ambiguous initializers. `const val` goes one step further: a compile-time constant, allowed only at top level or inside an `object`/`companion object`, inlined at every call site.

Nullability is part of the type in Kotlin: `String` can never hold null, `String?` can, and the compiler enforces the difference.

### Safe operators
- `?.` — safe call. Returns null when the receiver is null.
- `?:` — Elvis operator, supplies a default for null.
- `!!` — non-null assertion. Throws NullPointerException when null; treat every one as a bug waiting to happen.
- `?.let { ... }` — run the block only when non-null.
- `requireNotNull` / `checkNotNull` — fail fast with a message instead of a bare NPE.

When you interoperate with Java, types arrive as platform types (`String!`): Kotlin lets you use them either way and only fails at runtime, so annotate Java sources with @Nullable / @NonNull or convert at the boundary.

The K2 compiler, default since Kotlin 2.0, widened smart casts considerably — a null check now survives into more places, including a local `var` captured by a lambda and conditions combined with `||`. Less `!!` is needed than older tutorials suggest.

Kotlin's `List` is read-only, not immutable — the interface simply has no mutators, while the object behind it may be a MutableList somebody else can still change.

- `List<T>` vs `MutableList<T>` (add/remove/set).
- `Set<T>` vs `MutableSet<T>`.
- `Map<K, V>` vs `MutableMap<K, V>`.

### Factory functions
- `listOf`, `setOf`, `mapOf` — read-only.
- `mutableListOf`, `mutableSetOf`, `mutableMapOf` — mutable.
- `emptyList()`, `emptyMap()` — empty read-only.

Under the hood these wrap JDK collections, and the read-only types are interfaces rather than copies. Passing a MutableList where a `List` is expected is allowed; the consumer just cannot mutate through that reference. For a real guarantee use `kotlinx.collections.immutable` (`PersistentList`, `ImmutableList`) or copy defensively — Compose in particular relies on immutable collection types to keep parameters comparable.

Functional helpers (map / filter / reduce / fold / groupBy / chunked / windowed / partition) make data wrangling concise, and `asSequence()` turns a long chain lazy so it stops allocating an intermediate list per step.

Kotlin functions are first-class values — you can pass them as arguments, return them, and store them in variables.

- **Declaration**: `fun name(...): T = body` (single-expression) or `fun name(...) { ... }` (block body).
- **Default and named arguments** — fewer overloads to write.
- **Lambda**: `{ a, b -> a + b }`, with an implicit `it` for a single parameter.
- **Higher-order**: a function that takes or returns a function (`(Int) -> String`, `() -> Unit`).
- **Trailing-lambda convention**: `list.forEach { println(it) }`.
- **Function references**: `::isEven`, `String::length`, `User::name`.
- `inline` copies the body into the call site at compile time, removing the lambda allocation and enabling non-local return.

Kotlin idiom leans heavily on lambdas — collections, coroutines, Compose and every DSL are built out of them.

In Kotlin control structures are expressions — they produce a value and can sit on the right-hand side of an assignment or be returned directly.

- `if/else` — as an expression both branches are required. The result type is the least upper bound of the branch types.
- `when` — matches values, types (`is X`), ranges and collections (`in`), or arbitrary predicates when written without a subject. As an expression it must be exhaustive, either by covering a sealed / enum / Boolean type or through `else`.
- `try` is an expression too — `val n = try { input.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { 0 }`.
- A `when` STATEMENT over a sealed or enum subject must be exhaustive as well: that stopped being a warning and became an error in Kotlin 1.7.

Using them as expressions removes a lot of mutable state, because each branch produces the final value directly. Kotlin 2.1 added guard conditions, so a subject branch can carry an extra predicate: `is Cart if cart.isEmpty() -> ...`.

A smart cast is the compiler narrowing a value's type after a runtime check, so you never write the cast yourself.

- After `if (x is Type)` the compiler treats `x` as `Type` inside the block.
- After `if (x != null)` it treats `x` as non-nullable.
- It works in `when` branches and after an early `return` in the opposite branch.

A smart cast applies only when the compiler can prove the value did not change between check and use:
- `val` properties — always.
- A `var` of a class — never; the compiler cannot rule out another thread changing it between the check and the use, so it always treats the property as unsafe to narrow.
- Local variables and function parameters — generally yes.
- A mutable property of another object — no, another thread could change it between the two reads. Capture it into a local first.

The K2 compiler, default since Kotlin 2.0, made this noticeably smarter: a local `var` captured by a lambda, a value narrowed by a `||` condition, and a check inside an inline lambda now all smart-cast where the old front end gave up. When it still cannot prove safety, use `as` (throws on mismatch) or `as?` (returns null).

`==` compares content by calling `equals()`, while `===` asks whether two names point to the very same object.

- `a == b` compiles to `a?.equals(b) ?: (b === null)`, so it is null-safe on both sides and never throws. `!=` is its negation.
- `===` and `!==` are referential identity and cannot be overloaded. Two data-class instances with identical fields are `==` but not `===`.
- Overriding `equals()` changes what `==` means everywhere, so override `hashCode()` with it or hash-based collections start losing elements.

### Traps worth naming out loud
- Boxed numbers. `val a: Int? = 127; val b: Int? = 127` gives `a === b` true because of the JVM boxing cache, and the same code with 128 gives false. Never compare boxed primitives with `===`.
- Arrays. `==` on arrays is identity, not content — use `contentEquals()` or `contentDeepEquals()`.
- Floating point. When the static type is `Double`, `==` follows IEEE rules, so `NaN == NaN` is false. When the value is boxed or reached through a generic, `equals()` runs instead and reports `NaN` equal to itself and `0.0` different from `-0.0`.
code_example:
val a = User(1, "Ada")
val b = User(1, "Ada")
println(a == b)        // true  — data class equals
println(a === b)       // false — two objects

data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)

// Null-safe by construction
val s: String? = null
println(s == "hi")     // false, no NPE

// Boxing cache — the classic interview trick
val x: Int? = 127
val y: Int? = 127
println(x == y)        // true
println(x === y)       // true  (cached)
val p: Int? = 128
val q: Int? = 128
println(p == q)        // true
println(p === q)       // false (two boxes)

// Arrays compare by identity
val one = intArrayOf(1, 2)
val two = intArrayOf(1, 2)
println(one == two)            // false
println(one.contentEquals(two))// true

// equals and hashCode travel together
class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
  override fun equals(other: Any?) =
    other is Point && other.x == x && other.y == y
  override fun hashCode() = 31 * x + y
}

`lateinit var` is for a value somebody else hands you later, `by lazy` is for a value the property can compute itself on first read.

### `lateinit var`
- Only on a `var`, only on a non-null reference type — primitives are not allowed, so use `Delegates.notNull()` there.
- No custom getter or setter, and it cannot be a local variable of a top-level scope check.
- Reading it before assignment throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException, and `::prop.isInitialized` tells you whether it is safe to read.
- **Typical uses**: a view or binding assigned in `onCreate`, a field injected by Dagger or Hilt, a system under test built in `@Before`.

`by lazy { ... }`:
- Only on a `val`. The block runs at most once, on the first read, and the result is cached.
- Synchronized by default; `LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE` drops the lock when the property is confined to one thread.
- **Typical uses**: an expensive parser, a formatter, anything you may never touch on a given screen.

If neither fits, a plain nullable `var` with an explicit null check is honest and costs nothing. The one thing to avoid is `lateinit` on something that legitimately may be missing — that turns a real state into a crash.

Destructuring is positional — `val (a, b) = obj` calls the `component1()` and `component2()` operators in order, and the names you write are ignored.

### Where the `componentN` operators come from
- A `data class` gets one per primary-constructor property, in declaration order.
- `Map.Entry` and `Pair` / `Triple` have them, which is why `for ((key, value) in map)` reads so well.
- Any class can opt in by declaring `operator fun component1()` — including as an extension.

Everyday uses: `for ((index, item) in list.withIndex())`, `map.forEach { (k, v) -> ... }`, and multiple return values through a small data class instead of a `Pair` nobody can read.

The trap is exactly the positional part. Swap two same-typed properties in the primary constructor and every destructuring site still compiles, silently assigning the wrong values, and no test that only checks types will catch it. Guard against it by keeping destructuring to types with two or three obvious components, and reading wide models through their property names instead. Use `_` to skip a component you do not need, so a later reorder is at least less likely to line up.

Kotlin has no implicit widening between numeric types — every conversion is an explicit call such as `toLong()`.

- Smaller-to-larger assignment is rejected exactly like larger-to-smaller: write `itemCount.toLong()`.
- A literal is different. `val total: Long = 1` compiles because the compiler types the literal from the expected type; only an existing `Int` value needs the call.
- **Arithmetic still promotes**: `Int * Long` is a `Long`, and `Int / Int` is integer division, so `1 / 2` is 0 and `1.0 / 2` is 0.5.

### The conversions worth remembering
- `toInt()`, `toLong()`, `toDouble()` on any number, and on `String` where they throw NumberFormatException on bad input.
- `toIntOrNull()` / `toDoubleOrNull()` for anything a user typed — parse plus validation in one call.
- `Char` is not a number: use `char.code` for the code point and `char.digitToInt()` for a digit.

Two behaviours that bite in production: integer overflow wraps silently, so `Int.MAX_VALUE + 1` is negative rather than an exception — use `Long` for counters, milliseconds and money in minor units; and binary floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly, so never hold currency in a `Double`.

Yes — a `val` with a custom getter has no backing field and re-runs its body on every read, so only the absence of a setter is guaranteed.

### How properties actually work
- A Kotlin property is a getter, optionally a setter, and optionally a backing field. The compiler generates the field only when a default accessor is used or when the accessor mentions the special `field` identifier.
- `val isEmpty get() = size == 0` stores nothing: each read recomputes. `val id = nextId()` stores once.
- A custom setter reads and writes through `field`; writing `this.value = ...` inside it recurses until the stack overflows.
- `var count: Int = 0; private set` keeps the read public and the write internal to the class — the usual way to expose mutable state safely.

The practical consequences interviewers are looking for: a computed property must be cheap and free of side effects, because callers assume a read is nearly free — put anything expensive behind a function name like `computeTotal()` or cache it with `by lazy`. And a computed property is not part of a data class's `equals`, `hashCode` or `copy`, since those only see primary-constructor properties.

Nothing in a Kotlin signature tells the caller that a function can throw, so failure is either documented or moved into the return type.

### Language pieces you get
- `try` / `catch` / `finally` is an expression — `val n = try { s.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { 0 }`.
- `throw` has type `Nothing`, which is why it can sit in the branch of an expression without breaking type inference.
- `require(cond)` throws IllegalArgumentException for a bad argument, `check(cond)` throws IllegalStateException for a broken invariant, `error("msg")` always throws, and `requireNotNull` / `checkNotNull` return the value smart-cast to non-null.

### How to choose
- Programmer errors and truly exceptional conditions stay exceptions. A missing precondition is a bug, and crashing loudly in debug beats limping on.
- **Expected outcomes** — a wrong password, an offline device, a rejected payment — belong in the type: a `sealed interface` of Success and typed failures the caller must handle, or `Result<T>`.
- `runCatching { }` is the quick wrapper, but it catches every Throwable, so in coroutine code re-throw CancellationException before touching the result.
- Annotate with `@Throws` anything Java or Swift callers must catch, otherwise the interop layer sees a function that never throws.

`$` binds to the shortest identifier after it, so `"$user.name"` interpolates the whole `user` object and then appends the literal text `.name`.

- `$name` works only for a bare variable. Anything with a dot, an index or a call needs braces: `${user.name}`, `${items[0]}`, `${count + 1}`.
- A template calls `toString()`, and a null receiver renders the four characters `null` rather than throwing — that is how "Hello, null" ships to production. Write `${user?.name ?: "there"}`.
- `\$` escapes a dollar in a normal string. A raw string `"""..."""` has no escape sequences at all, so a literal dollar inside one is `${'$'}`.
- A raw string keeps the source indentation until you call `trimIndent()`, or `trimMargin()` when the lines start with `|`.

### Building strings
- The compiler lowers one template into a single efficient concatenation, but `result += part` inside a loop allocates a new String every iteration — JVM strings are immutable, so building an n-line report that way copies O(n²) characters.
- `buildString { append(...) }` hands you a StringBuilder scoped to the block and returns the finished string.
- `joinToString(", ") { it.title }` covers the usual case, with `prefix`, `postfix` and `limit` parameters instead of manual separator bookkeeping.

Rule of thumb: `$` for a bare variable, `${ }` the moment there is a dot, and `buildString` or `joinToString` the moment there is a loop.

`..` is inclusive at both ends, so `0..items.size` runs one step past the last valid index; the open-ended forms are `0..<items.size` (the `..<` operator, stable since Kotlin 1.9) and the older `0 until items.size`.

### The operators
- `a..b` — both ends included. `a..<b` / `a until b` — end excluded.
- `b downTo a` counts down and is inclusive; `step n` changes the stride; `reversed()` flips an existing range.
- A backwards `..` range is simply empty, not an error: `for (i in 5..1)` runs zero times and silently does nothing, which is why an accidentally reversed loop shows up as missing output rather than a crash.
- `in` / `!in` are membership tests that need no iteration at all: `if (code in 200..299)`, `when (age) { in 0..17 -> ... }`, `if (c in 'a'..'z')`. Any `Comparable` supports `in start..end`; only integral and `Char` ranges can be iterated.

### Iterating collections
- Prefer `for (item in items)`. When you need the position use `items.indices`, `items.lastIndex`, or `for ((i, item) in items.withIndex())`.
- `repeat(n) { }` when the counter is irrelevant.
- Removing from a list while a `for` loop iterates it throws ConcurrentModificationException — use `removeAll { }` or iterate `indices.reversed()`.

Written directly in the loop header, `for (i in 0..<n)` compiles to a plain int loop with no iterator and no boxing; the same range put through `.map { }` allocates a full list.

The plain name asserts that the element exists and throws when it does not; the `OrNull` suffix is the question form that hands back null instead.

### The pairs worth knowing
- `first()` / `last()` throw NoSuchElementException; `firstOrNull()` / `lastOrNull()` do not. `find { }` is already `firstOrNull { }`.
- `list[i]` throws IndexOutOfBoundsException; `getOrNull(i)` and `getOrElse(i) { default }` do not.
- `single()` throws NoSuchElementException on empty and IllegalArgumentException when there is more than one match. `singleOrNull()` returns null in **both** cases, so it quietly hides the "two matches" bug you were trying to catch.
- `max()` / `min()` were removed in Kotlin 1.5 and reintroduced in 1.7 with a non-null return that throws on an empty collection; `maxOrNull()`, `maxByOrNull { }` and `maxOfOrNull { }` are the safe forms.
- On a map, `map[key]` returns null, `getValue(key)` throws NoSuchElementException, and `getOrElse(key) { }` / `getOrPut(key) { }` cover the rest.

### What empty means per operation
- `sum()` on an empty list is 0, `average()` is `NaN`, `reduce { }` throws, `fold(init) { }` returns `init`.
- `joinToString()` gives an empty string, not null.

Rule of thumb: at a boundary — network, database, user input — use the `OrNull` form with an Elvis and decide what empty means. Keep the throwing form where an empty collection would genuinely be a bug, so it fails loudly at the source instead of three screens later.

A default value belongs to the declaration, not to the call: the Kotlin compiler fills it in at each call site, so overriding code, Java code and code compiled earlier all see a different function than you do.

### How the mechanism works
- Defaults are evaluated on every call, in declaration order, and a later default may reference an earlier parameter: `fun retry(times: Int = 3, delayMs: Long = times * 100L)`. A `= mutableListOf()` default therefore produces a fresh list per call — Kotlin has no shared-mutable-default trap.
- An **override may not repeat a default**. The base declaration owns the value, the override just inherits it, and the value used is the one from the static type you call through — which is precisely why the language forbids a subclass from redefining it.
- Positional arguments come first; from Kotlin 1.4 you may name an argument in its own position and keep passing the rest positionally. Naming is how you skip a middle default: `load(id, retries = 5)`.

### What it costs on a public API
- Java sees only the full signature plus a synthetic `load$default` bridge. Add `@JvmOverloads` to generate the real telescoping overloads — mandatory for a custom `View` constructor that Android inflates from XML.
- Adding a parameter changes the JVM signature even when it has a default, so a module compiled against the old version fails at runtime with NoSuchMethodError until it is rebuilt. Inside one app that is invisible; for a published library it is a breaking change.
- Inserting a same-typed parameter in the middle keeps every positional call compiling while silently changing what those arguments mean. Append new parameters at the end, or force named arguments.

`forEach` is an inline function, so its lambda body is compiled into your function and a bare `return` is a real return from *your* function — skipping a single item is `return@forEach`.

### What the compiler does
- Inlining copies the lambda into the call site, which is what makes a non-local return possible at all: there is no separate frame to return from, so `return` targets the enclosing function.
- Every lambda gets an implicit label named after the function it was passed to. `return@forEach` finishes this iteration and behaves like `continue`; `return@map value` supplies this element's result.
- Loops take explicit labels for the same reason: `outer@ for (...) { for (...) { break@outer } }`.
- `let`, `run`, `apply`, `also` and `takeIf` are inline too, which is why the early-exit idiom `user?.let { return save(it) }` works.

### Where a bare return is refused
- A lambda passed to a **non-inline** function, stored in a variable, or declared `crossinline` cannot use a bare `return` — it may run after the enclosing function has already finished, so the compiler rejects it and only a labeled return to an explicit label compiles.
- An anonymous function, `fun(item: Item) { return }`, always returns from itself and needs no label.

`forEach` also has no `break`. When you want to stop iterating, say so directly: `firstOrNull { }`, `any { }`, `none { }`, or a plain `for` loop with `break`.

`throw` is an expression of type `Nothing`, the bottom of Kotlin's type hierarchy and a subtype of every other type, so it fits into a branch that has to produce a `String`.

### The three special types
- `Any?` is the top type; `Any` is the root of the non-null types and declares only `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`.
- `Unit` is an ordinary singleton object returned by functions with nothing better to give back. A lambda whose expected type ends in `-> Unit` discards its last expression, which is why `forEach { seen.add(it) }` compiles even though `add` returns a `Boolean`.
- `Nothing` has no instances at all. `throw`, `TODO()`, `error()` and `exitProcess()` are typed `Nothing`, so the compiler knows control never returns and marks the code after them unreachable. A helper declared `fun fail(msg: String): Nothing` can therefore be used as a `when` branch without widening the result type. `Nothing?` has exactly one value — null — which is why `val x = null` infers `Nothing?` and `emptyList()` (a `List<Nothing>`) is assignable to any `List<T>`.

### Checking and casting
- `is` / `!is` test and smart-cast; `as` throws ClassCastException; `as?` yields null, so pair it with an Elvis.
- Generic arguments are erased on the JVM. `value as List<String>` only checks "is a List", the compiler warns about an unchecked cast, and the ClassCastException surfaces later at the first element read — far from the cast that caused it. Use `filterIsInstance<String>()` or an `inline fun <reified T>` helper instead.
code_example:
fun requireId(raw: String?): String =
    raw ?: throw IllegalStateException("no id")   // `throw` is Nothing, a subtype of String

fun loadConfig(): Config = TODO("wire the remote config")  // TODO() is Nothing too

fun fail(msg: String): Nothing = throw IllegalArgumentException(msg)

val level: Int = when (raw) {
    "high" -> 2
    "low" -> 0
    else -> fail("bad level: $raw")   // Nothing branch, `when` still typed Int
}

// Nothing? has exactly one value
val nothing = null                    // inferred Nothing?
val empty: List<String> = emptyList() // List<Nothing> fits any List<T>

// Any is the root of the non-null hierarchy
val boxed: Any = 42
val text = boxed as? String ?: "not a string"   // as? instead of a crash

// A `-> Unit` lambda throws its result away
val seen = mutableSetOf<String>()
val record: (String) -> Unit = { seen.add(it) } // add() returns Boolean, coerced to Unit

// Erasure: this cast only checks "is a List"
val cache: Map<String, Any> = loadCache()
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
val ids = cache["ids"] as List<String>          // ❌ blows up later, at the first read
val safeIds = (cache["ids"] as? List<*>).orEmpty().filterIsInstance<String>()  // ✅

inline fun <reified T> Map<String, Any>.typed(key: String): T? = this[key] as? T

Arrays inherit Java's identity `equals`, so `==` on two arrays compares references, not contents — content comparison is `contentEquals` (`contentDeepEquals` for nested arrays).

### What arrays do differently
- `toString()` prints `[Ljava.lang.String;@1b6d3586`; the readable form is `contentToString()`.
- `hashCode` is identity-based too, so a `data class` with an `Array` property gets a generated `equals`/`hashCode` that ignores the contents. The IDE warns about it; hold a `List` instead, or hand-write both accessors.
- `Array<T>` is an object array, so `Array<Int>` is `Integer[]` and boxes every element. `IntArray`, `LongArray`, `DoubleArray`, `BooleanArray`, `ByteArray` and `CharArray` map to real Java primitive arrays.
- Arrays have a fixed size and are **invariant** in Kotlin: `Array<String>` is not an `Array<Any>`. Java made arrays covariant and pays for it with ArrayStoreException at runtime; Kotlin moved that error to compile time.

### Where an array is still the right type
- `vararg` parameters are arrays, and you forward one with the spread operator `*parts`.
- `main(args: Array<String>)`, `ByteArray` for IO and crypto, primitive-heavy numeric code, and any Java or Android API that demands one.
- Cross over with `toList()`, `toIntArray()`, `toTypedArray()`.

Everywhere else `List` is the default: it prints, compares and hashes the way you expect.
code_example:
val a = arrayOf("x", "y")
val b = arrayOf("x", "y")

println(a == b)              // false — identity equals, inherited from Any
println(a.contentEquals(b))  // true
println(a.toString())        // [Ljava.lang.String;@1b6d3586
println(a.contentToString()) // [x, y]

// ❌ generated equals/hashCode compare the array by reference
data class Payload(val bytes: ByteArray)
println(Payload(byteArrayOf(1)) == Payload(byteArrayOf(1)))  // false

// ✅ hold a List, or write both accessors by hand
data class SafePayload(val bytes: List<Byte>)

// Boxed vs primitive
val boxed: Array<Int> = arrayOf(1, 2, 3)   // Integer[] — one box per element
val raw: IntArray = intArrayOf(1, 2, 3)    // int[]
val zeros = IntArray(4)                    // [0, 0, 0, 0]
val squares = Array(4) { it * it }         // [0, 1, 4, 9]

// Fixed size and invariant
// val any: Array<Any> = arrayOf("x")      // ❌ Array<String> is not Array<Any>
// Java allows exactly this and throws ArrayStoreException at runtime instead

// Where arrays are unavoidable
fun log(vararg parts: String) = println(parts.joinToString(" "))
val parts = arrayOf("a", "b")
log(*parts)                                // spread operator

val bytes: ByteArray = file.readBytes()
val asList = raw.toList()
val backToArray = asList.toIntArray()
val typed = listOf("a", "b").toTypedArray()

`if` needs a real `Boolean` and `Boolean?` has three states, so you cannot write the condition until you decide what null means — and `== true`, `?: false` both decide it means false.

- `flag == true` is false when null; `flag != false` is true when null; `flag ?: false` and `flag ?: true` say the same thing more explicitly. `!!` claims null is impossible and crashes when the backend disagrees.
- Negation is where the bug hides: `!(flag == true)` is true for null, while `flag == false` is not. Over three states those are different questions.
- `&&` and `||` do not accept nullable operands, so collapse each side first: `a?.enabled == true && b?.enabled == true`.
- When null genuinely means "not loaded yet", branch on it: `when (flag) { true -> ...; false -> ...; null -> ... }` is exhaustive over `Boolean?` and the compiler will keep it that way.

### Helpers that already accept null
- `isNullOrBlank()`, `isNullOrEmpty()` and `orEmpty()` are declared on nullable receivers, so no `?.` is needed — `!name.isNullOrBlank()` reads better than `name?.isNotBlank() == true`.
- `mapNotNull { }`, `filterNotNull()` and `listOfNotNull(a, b)` drop nulls instead of guarding each element.

The real fix is at the boundary: give the DTO field a non-null type with a default, or map the DTO into a domain model with non-null types, so three-valued logic never reaches the UI layer.
